bio.en: Benedict Evans is a long-time analyst (formerly in-house at a16z) and independent thinker who has tracked the most important shifts in tech and now writes about where the industry is heading.
bio.zh: Benedict Evans 是资深分析师（曾为 a16z 驻场分析师）和独立思想家，长期追踪科技行业最重要的变化，如今撰写关于行业走向的文章。

summary.en: Benedict argues AI is as big a deal as the internet or mobile—but only that big—and pushes back on “job apocalypse” panic, noting every new technology automates some jobs while unlocking new ones we can't yet imagine. He cautions against head-in-the-sand denial and advises people to dive in and learn what AI can actually do. The conversation is a clear-eyed take on hype, history, and how to position yourself for an AI-shaped future.
summary.zh: Benedict 认为 AI 与互联网或移动端同等重要——但也“仅此而已”——并反驳“就业末日”的恐慌，指出每项新技术在自动化部分工作的同时，也会解锁我们尚无法想象的新工作。他警示不要掩耳盗铃式地否认，并建议人们深入其中、学习 AI 真正能做什么。对话对炒作、历史以及如何在 AI 塑造的未来中定位自己给出了清醒的判断。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: My most controversial opinion is that I think that AI is as big a deal as the internet or mobile, and only as big a deal as the internet or mobile.
turns.zh: 我最具争议的观点是，我认为人工智能的重要性堪比互联网和移动技术，而且其影响力也仅次于这两者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But you're just on the coming job apocalypse.
turns.zh: 但你正身处即将到来的就业末日。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Every time we have a new technology, it automates away a bunch of jobs. And then that automation unlocks a bunch of new jobs. And you don't know the new job because it doesn't exist yet. We've had that process over and over again.
turns.zh: 每次新技术出现，都会淘汰大量工作岗位。随后，技术革新又会创造出新的就业机会。但这些新岗位在诞生前，你根本无法预见其存在。我们一次又一次地经历着这样的循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Even just looking at the most advanced AI companies, throughout big OpenAI, everyone's increasing headcount.
turns.zh: 即便看看最先进的人工智能公司，包括大型的OpenAI，每家公司都在增加员工数量。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: You talk to these doomers on Twitter and they would act like every big company is going to buy ChatGPT tomorrow, and then in two weeks' time, they'll fire all their stuff. These people are more on. You can't predict which things are going to be exposed. You can't look at a senior partner at a law firm and say, "Well, 17% of their work could be automated." This is horseshit.
turns.zh: 你在推特上与那些悲观论者交谈时，他们总是一副所有大公司明天就会购买ChatGPT，两周后就裁掉所有员工的架势。这些人想得太消极了。你无法预测哪些工作会被自动化取代。你不能对律师事务所的资深合伙人说：“好吧，他们17%的业务可以实现自动化。”这简直是胡说八道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious if you're following the anti-AI sentiment.
turns.zh: 我很好奇你是否关注反人工智能的情绪。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: It's a big fuzzy mess. Yes, this will change a bunch of stuff and we'll need to worry about it, but that's kind of a constant. We've always had that.
turns.zh: 这是一团混乱的乱麻。是的，人工智能将改变很多东西，我们需要为此担忧，但这种担忧是持续存在的。我们一直如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What would be a couple things you recommend people do to be more successful in this future?
turns.zh: 对于未来要想更成功，你会建议人们做些什么？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Don't stick your head in the sand and say, "I hate all of this stuff." That gives you a great feeling of all superiority and you can go on BlueSky and chat at everybody about how Evil AI is like, great, happy for you. But that's not going to help. What helps is you diving into this and coming out, understanding what you can do with it.
turns.zh: 别把头埋在沙子里说：“我讨厌这一切。”这样会让你自视甚高，去BlueSky上和大家聊聊“邪恶的人工智能”有多棒，为你点赞。但这没用。真正有用的做法是深入研究，理解你能用它做些什么。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: An interesting way of thinking about it, I did a podcast last year with someone where I said my most controversial opinion is that I think that AI is as big a deal as the internet or mobile. The internet was quite a big deal. We wouldn't be doing this if it wasn't for the internet. And the people who've already got it, who have already taken whichever pill it is, I forget which, sort of imagine that everybody in the world is already there. And has OpenAI won the whole thing? Or is Anthropic got it this week? (00:04:46): So there's a fractual point here. There's the super high level that this is going to change absolutely everything. I do a presentation every six months and I just published one yesterday, and one of the comments was, "Benedict, this is 80 slides of saying we don't know," which is slightly facetious, but also kind of true.
turns.zh: 这是一个很有趣的思考方式。去年我做了一期播客，期间我说了自己最具争议的观点：我认为AI的重要性堪比互联网或移动技术。但仅限于此，因为显然有很多科技从业者认为，这更像是工业革命之类的变革。还有很多人在底下评论：“他觉得这和……一样重要？他难道不明白这有多重要吗？” 而我会回应：智能手机就曾引发巨大变革。互联网同样意义非凡。没有互联网，我们根本无法开展当下的工作。（00:03:19）但如果你深入探讨，将其与互联网作比较的话，我们正处于1997年的阶段。当时令人兴奋不已，但多数功能尚未实现。人们计划开展的大多数应用尚未开发出来，即便开发出来，其运作机制也尚不明朗。而那些已经拥抱AI、提前尝到甜头的人（我记不清是哪家公司了），总想象全世界的人都已经跟上了步伐。但现实是，AI的应用范围极为广泛。有些科技公司购买了Mac mini集群，却不再使用谷歌服务；而在科技领域之外，除了那些否认其真实性的傻瓜外，大多数用户每周都会使用相关技术。（00:04:12）因此，应用普及度和成熟度存在巨大差异。比如模型如何运行？模型实验室是否拥有定价权？价值将流向何处？OpenAI是否已经胜出？Anthropic本周又是否会脱颖而出？这就像1997年时人们争论“Excite和雅虎谁会胜出”一样。当时的答案显然是否定的。（00:04:46）所以这里存在一个分裂点。一方面，人们坚信AI将彻底改变一切。但用“比互联网大20%还是100%”来争论毫无意义。这类讨论毫无益处。但这确实是一场根本性变革，而其具体运作机制尚不明朗。事实上，我刚刚发布了相关内容。我每六个月做一次演示，昨天刚发布了一次，其中有人评论道：“本尼迪克特，这80页PPT全在说我们还不知道。” 这话带点调侃，但也不无道理。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Well, unquestionably, we are already in that moment in software, and then there's a conversation about, well, what does Agentic and AI software development, three separate things that merge together, mean for the future of the software industry? There's one extreme which is no one really believes, which is, "hey, you'll just vibe create your in Stripe." (00:07:40): One of the analogies I used in the presentation is, imagine you're an accountant seeing the first software spreadsheets in the late '70s, and this is mind-blowing. (00:09:34): And all of those intersect with your software developer. 嗯，毫无疑问，我们已经身处软件行业的这个转折点了。随之而来的，是关于Agentic和AI软件开发的讨论——这三者合并在一起，将对软件行业的未来意味着什么？一种极端观点是，没人真的相信“嘿，你只需在Stripe上随意创建应用”这种说法。虽然短期内你可能这么想，但显然大多数人对这意味着什么、能自行完成多少工作、未来会有多少软件产生等问题心存疑虑。这是整个讨论的核心议题。但另一种极端观点是，如果你身处律师事务所，所有这些新技术固然很有趣，但如何有效应用呢？如何避免重蹈覆辙，比如上次提交文件时因人为失误导致的混乱？明年又要招聘多少助理律师？这对我们意味着什么？（00:07:40）  
我在演讲中用过的一个类比是：想象你是一名会计师，在70年代末首次接触电子表格。这简直令人惊叹——你只需更改利率，其他数据就会自动更新。它能在30秒内完成一周的工作量。显然，这对会计行业意义非凡。但如果你是一名律师或记者，你可能只会想：“这技术挺酷的，我的会计应该看看。”但这毕竟不是你的专业领域。除非你愿意花1万到1.5万美元购买苹果II电脑、显示器和打印机来运行它，否则根本没法实际应用。更别提你还需要文字处理软件，而文字处理软件不久后就问世了。（00:08:26）  
这正是我们所处的历史节点：有些人（比如软件开发者）像当年看到VisiCalc的会计师一样惊呼“天哪，这一切都将改变”。VisiCalc之前和之后，Claude Code之前和之后。许多其他人也在不同程度上尝试使用这些技术，但仍心存疑虑。演讲中引用的调查数据显示，即便在13至18岁这样的年轻群体中，仍有15%至20%的人每天活跃使用，还有20%的人每周使用。其余60%的人则表示不使用这些技术。（00:09:09）  
这种技术的普及程度参差不齐，这也映射出一个复杂的边界问题：它在哪些领域有效？哪些领域无效？你能预测它将应用于何处？它是否直观易懂？它成功后你能否复现？你能否自己设计应用场景？（00:09:34）  
所有这些问题都与软件开发者息息相关。许多其他人要么对新技术心存疑虑，要么正处于类似1997年“好吧，这是什么？”的探索阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, something you've been writing a bit about is, this unexpected investment in professional services/consulting services/forward deployed engineers, all the AI labs, at least the two big ones, OpenAI and Anthropic, are investing in buying massive consultancies and PE firms. Talk about just what's happening there, why that's happening.
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，你在文章中提到的一个观点是，OpenAI和Anthropic等两大人工智能实验室正大规模投资收购咨询公司和私募股权公司，比如Accenture和Infosys。能否详细解析一下这种现象背后的原因？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Well, it's funny, I was kind of groping for a joke last night when I wrote my newsletter and couldn't quite get to land it. But something like, we know the joke that a machine learning scientist is a statistician who lives in San Francisco. And there's something in there of like a forward deployed engineer is like an Accenture outsource software developer who lives in San Francisco, or works in San Francisco. I mean, joking apart, if you have any experience of professional services, companies do not have lots of people sitting around waiting to build a big new project, or do a big new piece of analysis, or build a big new piece of technology, or a new product, or work out how they're going to redesign their stores, or work out where the store should be, or try and work out why the churn is too high. All of those kinds of questions are reasons why you hire Bain, BCG, McKinsey on one side, or Accenture, Infosys, whoever on the other, or you hire a branding agency, or you hire an arch firm of architects or whatever. (00:11:09): And it's always like, well, we could hire some architects, but why on earth would we want to have 15 architects on staff when we would just go and hire an architecture firm, and we just go and hire an ad agency? And so we are supposed to completely reimagine all of the internal workflows of your company, and work out which of them could be automated really quickly with AI. That's a project. That's a project that needs like five or 10 people to sit down and spend a month or two working it out. And then actually doing it is another project. (00:11:39): Okay, so you need to plug these three vertical systems into these two horizontal systems and build a bunch of new workflows and train people to do that. Well, guess what? Who's going to do that? Because you don't have a bunch of people sitting around not doing anything. So, on the one side, this is part of the model of some PE firms, which is that they provide support to their portfolio companies to do stuff. And on the other side, that's why you hire, depending on what you're trying to do, you hire Bain, or you hire Accenture, or you hire publicists to help you work that out.
turns.zh: 说起来挺有意思的，我昨晚写新闻通讯时还想找个笑料，但没成功。不过有个梗，叫“机器学习科学家是住在旧金山的统计学家”。类似的，“前沿部署工程师”可以理解为住在旧金山的埃森哲外包软件开发者之类的。说正经的，如果你有过专业服务经验，就会知道公司不会闲着等着开发新项目、做新分析、研发新技术、推出新产品，或者重新设计门店、选址、分析客户流失率。这些问题正是你找Bain、BCG、麦肯锡等咨询公司，或者Accenture、Infosys等外包服务商的原因。（00:11:09）但现在的情况是，人们会想：“我们可以招几个建筑师，但为什么要养15个全职建筑师团队？直接找专业事务所不是更省心吗？”同样，广告代理也是如此。（00:11:39）要重新构想公司内部流程，梳理哪些环节能快速用AI自动化，这本身就是个需要五到十人团队花一两个月才能完成的项目。真正落地执行更是难上加难。（00:12:11）所以你需要把三个垂直系统接入两个横向系统，建立新流程并培训员工。这时候问题来了：谁来做这些事？毕竟公司里不可能闲着大量人手。所以一方面，PE公司会为投资组合公司提供支持；另一方面，你需要根据具体需求选择Bain、Accenture或公关公司来协助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's really just funny about this trend is you would think consultants were going to be gone. No, we don't need all these people anymore. AI is going to do their work. Instead, the most cutting edge AI labs are the ones most investing in these folks. I think it's pretty surprising.
turns.zh: 这个趋势最有趣的地方在于，你可能以为咨询公司会被淘汰。毕竟AI能替代他们的工作。相反，最前沿的AI实验室反而在大力投资这些资源。这确实令人惊讶。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Well, one of the strands in my presentation, so I split the presentation into three sections. There's a section on capital, which is basically, where is all this CapEx going and are the model labs going to have differentiation? And then there's a section on deployment, which is basically, what does it mean for the software industry? And then the third section is, how does this change stuff? And one of the sort of strands I tried to pull together in the section on change is, what's the hard part of the job? Is the hard part of the job writing the code line by line? Is the hard part of the job giving you the SKU, or making the PowerPoint? Or is the hard part of the job something else? Is it the task or the job? (00:13:11): And pulling that apart, sometimes the task is the job. The classic example is like an elevator attendant. If I live in a building that has an attended elevator, we have a manual elevator, so there's no button. There's a lever and the dormant drives you to your floor. It's a vertical speed cut. It's like one of those cramps in San Francisco. They drive you to the store, to your floor. And then those all got automated after the '50s, and now you press a button, and pressing the button is a job. So there were some things where the button, the job was a task and the task got automated. What happens much more, and this is why people talked about the Jevons paradox is this pricey elasticity, because the Jevons paradox is just price elasticity, applied price elasticity. If you make it cheaper to do something, what happens? Do you do the same for less money? Or do you do more for the same amount of money? Or do you do more for more money because you've got new ROI? (00:14:00): And if you look at something like the history of accounting, or indeed professional services, this is a joke I made on Twitter back when it was Twitter, was like, young people won't believe this, but before Excel, junior investment bankers worked really long hours. And now thanks to Excel, Goldman's associates will work at lunchtime on Fridays. It's like, well, why is that not what happened? You could make the same point as software development. Before IDEs, and libraries, and operating systems, developers had to write all the code. Now if you write an iPhone app, 90% of the code is written for you by Apple. Apple wrote the modem driver, and the graphics drivers, and the file system. You don't need to write any of that. So, we've got intents as many engineers now. Well, no. And so then you kind of have to look at an industry and work out, well, which is it and what is the hard part? (00:14:48): One of the analogies that occurred to me here is to look at the history of e-commerce, which is that what Amazon does is it gets you the SKU if you know what the SKU is. If you know what SKU you want, you want that microphone stand. This part number, you can go to Amazon and get it. If you don't know what microphone to get, probably shouldn't start on Amazon. (00:15:11): Multiply that by many, many, many product categories. And so what Amazon does is get you the SKU, but knowing what SKU you want is another job. Claude Code can write you the code, but what code do you want? It can make you the features. Sure, but what features do you want? Who's your customer? What's the right product for that customer? How are you going to take it to market? And long way of answering a question, why do you hire McKinsey? Are you hiring them to get a 75-slide deck? Well, narrowly, Claude cowork will make a really, really crappy version of that. And you'll get all this kind of AI grifters on LinkedIn and Twitter and so on saying, "Hey, I made a McKinsey deck with Claude," and you look at it and you think, "Yeah, that's a bunch of doc crap." That's not what you'd get from McKinsey. (00:15:54): But even if it was, that's not what you paid them for. What you actually pay Bain to do is to go and walk all over your company and work out. Yes, but why is it that you didn't do that? And how do the politics of this work? And what do you actually need to do? And let's go and talk to your customers and work out what they actually think, as opposed to what's on the first page of Google. It's all the other stuff. And the PowerPoint is just like the task, but that's not what you hired them for. The same with Amazon versus the retailer, the same with software development. So you've got that kind of split. (00:16:29): The other analogy that occurred to me here is looking at the sort of class of industry that got steamrolled by the internet, because they had those two things and you could split the part. So you had the physical manufacturing or physical distribution, and then you had the other, the thing, what was the actual thing? Classic examples would be newspapers and recorded music. So record companies do not think of themselves as being in the business of manufacturing small pieces of plastic, but that was what they actually did. And when that went away, they were screwed. (00:16:58): Same thing with newspapers. Newspapers did not think of themselves as manufacturing. And trucking companies. When you decouple that, then that becomes a problem. But often you can't decouple that, or that wasn't really the problem; or you make that thing cheap and then all this other stuff happens as well. And so all of this is just vastly more complicated than saying, "Well, hey, we're just going to automate the accountants or we're going to automate the consultants." I mean, there's two charts in the presentation of the number of people employed as accountants, which went up right the way through the 20th century, and has gone up again since the beginning of the 21st century. So you have adding machines, and punch cards, and mainframes, and databases, and ERP, and cloud, with spreadsheets and PCs, and the number of accountants keep going up. And so why is that? Well, it's more complicated than automation.
turns.zh:
嗯，我演讲的核心内容主要分为三个部分。第一部分是关于资本的，主要探讨所有这些资本支出流向何处，以及模型实验室是否会形成差异化。第二部分是关于部署的，重点在于这对软件行业意味着什么。第三部分是关于变革的，试图解析工作的核心挑战——是逐行编写代码？还是处理SKU编号？又或者是制作PPT？归根结底，工作的核心在于任务而非职位。

（00:13:11）：具体来说，有时候任务本身就是工作。典型的例子是电梯管理员。如果我住在有电梯管理员的楼里，电梯是手动操作的，没有按钮，只有操控杆来控制楼层。这就像旧金山的缆车——被自动化取代后，人们按下按钮，按钮本身从任务变成了工作。

（00:14:00）：回到专业服务领域，比如会计史。推特时代我曾调侃过，年轻人难以置信，但在Excel出现前，投行新人加班到深夜。现在得益于Excel，金曼的员工周五午餐时间就能下班了。这就引出了一个问题：为何结果并非如此？软件开发同样面临挑战。在IDE、库和操作系统出现前，开发者需要手动编写所有代码。如今开发iPhone应用，90%代码由苹果完成。苹果编写了调制解调器驱动、图形驱动和文件系统，无需开发者重复造轮子。

（00:15:11）：以电商为例，亚马逊提供SKU查询服务，但用户必须知道SKU编号。若用户明确想要某个麦克风支架，通过编号就能找到。反之，若用户毫无头绪，恐怕难以在亚马逊下单。

（00:16:13）：将这种模式复制到无数产品类别中。亚马逊的核心价值在于提供SKU，但找到合适SKU本身就是另一项任务。Claude Code可以编写代码，但用户需要明确需求。亚马逊提供功能，但用户必须明确需求。用户是谁？适合哪种产品？如何推向市场？长篇大论回答一个问题：为何聘请麦肯锡？麦肯锡能做75页PPT？Claude Cowork只能做个劣质版本。
领英和推特上到处都是这样的人，他们会发帖说：“嘿，我和克劳德一起做了一份麦肯锡的演示文稿。”但你看过后会觉得：“是啊，不过那不过是些劣质PPT罢了。” 这可不是麦肯锡应有的水准。（00:15:54）但即便如此，这也不是你花钱请他们来做的。你请贝恩公司来做的，是深入你的公司进行全面诊断。没错，但你为什么没有这么做呢？这背后的权力博弈是怎样的？你真正需要做的是什么？让我们去和你的客户聊聊，了解他们的真实想法，而不是从谷歌首页搜出来的那些信息。关键在于其他方面。PPT只是任务的一部分，但这并非你雇佣他们的初衷。亚马逊与传统零售商的竞争，以及软件开发领域的类似情况，都体现了这种分野。（00:16:29）我想到的另一个类比，是那些被互联网彻底颠覆的行业。这些行业本质上可以拆分成两个部分：一个是实体制造或实体分销，另一个是什么来着？典型例子就是报纸和录制音乐。唱片公司从不认为自己从事的是制造小塑料片的业务，但这正是他们的实际业务。当这种业务消失时，他们就完蛋了。（00:16:58）报纸行业也是如此。报社从不认为自己是制造业。还有货运公司。当你将这些环节割裂开时，问题就出现了。但往往你无法割裂这些环节，或者这根本不是问题所在；或者你让某个环节成本降低，但随之而来的其他问题也会接踵而至。所以，所有这些问题都比简单地说“我们要把会计自动化”或“我们要把顾问自动化”要复杂得多。演示文稿中有一张图表，显示20世纪雇佣会计师的数量持续增长，进入21世纪后又再度攀升。从加法机、打孔卡、主机、数据库、ERP到云计算，再到电子表格和个人电脑，雇佣的会计师数量不断增加。为什么会这样？这比自动化要复杂得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Even just looking at the most advanced AI companies, Anthropic, OpenAI, I just had Dan Shipper from Every on the podcast, everyone's just increasing headcount. The companies you would think would be least likely to add humans are adding many, many humans. And since your point, it's really complicated. What you're just kind just on the job, the coming job apocalypse, like Dario's talking about all the entry level people are no more jobs, just like...
turns.zh: 即便只看最先进的人工智能公司，比如Anthropic、OpenAI，我最近在播客上采访了Every的丹·希珀，每家公司都在不断扩充团队规模。那些你可能认为最不愿意增聘人力的公司，实际上却在大量招人。这就回到了你提出的那个问题——这确实很复杂。就拿你提到的就业问题，未来很可能迎来一场就业危机，正如达里奥所言，许多初级岗位将消失，取而代之的将是……

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, there's a narrow point here, which is that I would place... I don't like argument from authority. And I don't think the fact that you run AI lab suddenly gives you... Or rather, if you're going to use argument from authority, then it should be relevant to the field. So, I'm interested in Dario's opinions on where models are going to go in the next six to 12 months. I'm not particularly interested in it opinions on series of labor and market value and comparative advantage. Yeah, maybe he had a course on that at university, so did I. So, I think one needs to be a little bit cautious on what Dario says. And that's setting aside the cynical view that he's just doing that department stock, which I don't believe at all. (00:18:50): So this kind of comes back to my point about platform shifts. Every time we have a new technology, it automates away a bunch of jobs. And then that automation, whether it's price elasticity, and the enablement of the fact that they became automated, unlock so much of new jobs. And so you go back to 1800, 90% of us were peasants, and our major concern was like, are the crops going to fail? Because then we'll all go hungry. Or worse. And so ever since then, we've been automating jobs and creating new jobs, and you can always see the job that's going to go away, and you don't know the new job because it doesn't exist yet, and it's like something that sounds dumb anyway. Like railway engineer, what's a railway? Why would that be a thing? Who would want to go that fast? And so we've had that process over and over again. This is what any first-year economic student would tell you. We've had this process over and over again since 1800. (00:19:41): And each time you go through it, you get a bunch of frictional pain and dislocation, and a bunch of people do their jobs, and a bunch of towns get hollowed out, and it all sucks. But when you come through on the other side, we're all richer, and we're not worried about the crops failing anymore. And this is the process of the last 200 years. So then the question is, is there some a primary reason why this would be different to those? Because the internet removed a bunch of jobs, PCs removed a bunch of jobs. There aren't many people working as typesetters anymore. Or telephone operators, or typists. The internet removed a bunch of jobs. And generally the jobs that go away are crap jobs, seen retrospectively, and the new job, the better, because GDP keeps going up. (00:20:19): So, is AI different? And so then there's kind of a couple of answers to this. One theory is, well, this is going to be way quicker. And certainly the adoption of AI is quicker than previous technologies, but this is kind of because you're turning on the shoulders of giants. So you don't need to wait for everyone to buy a piece of expensive hardware, to buy a phone or a PC, or wait for the telco to deploy broadband. That's already there. So of course, ChatGPT can get 900 million chat users, because there's already 900 million people on the internet. When Mark Andreessen launched Netscape in what was it, '93, '94, there were like 50 to 100 million PCs on earth. So now you didn't have 900 million users then. But the point is then he didn't need to wait for phone networks or microchips. And before that, you didn't need to wait for electricity, and you didn't need to wait for mass production. So you're always standing on the shoulders of giants. There's always a compounding effect. So yeah, this is faster, but the internet was faster too. (00:21:11): I think the other answer to this, and this kind of comes back to the professional services point is, you talk to these doomers on Twitter, and they would act like every big company is going to buy ChatGPT tomorrow, and then in two weeks time, they'll fire all their staff, and these people are mourners. This is one of many reasons why the doomers were mourns, but complete failure to understand the way the world works. And that was like the starting point why they then didn't understand anything else. Turn to a big company, enterprise software sales cycle, you'll know this better than me, enterprise software sales cycle is like 18 months, if you're lucky. This is always a problem. The enterprise sales cycle is shorter than the venture backed funding cycle. Longer rather. Longer. It takes you longer to get an enterprise deal than it takes you to go between raps. And this was always supporting the building, particularly for sectors like aerospace, or healthcare, or something. (00:21:57): So, I know people aren't just going to tear out SAP and replace it with X, Y, Z. Maybe in like three, five, 10 years, yes, that whole estate will look radically different, and all those jobs will have changed, but it will take two, three, four, five, 10 years, and it will take time sector by sector, and it will take time for people to work out, "You could do that thing with this." (00:22:19): And one of the companies I always remember that we looked at when I was at Andreessen Horowitz is a company called Frame.io, which is video editing, video collaboration. And there's nothing there that you couldn't have done at least five years earlier, and maybe 10 years earlier. And actually, that's kind of a bad example because that relies on a bunch of stuff like cutting edge web technologies. But if you go out and pick 10 random SaaS companies that were started the day before ChatGPT launched, how many of them could have been founded at any point in the previous 15 years? (00:22:54): The delay was somebody realizing, "Oh, that problem exists inside that industry, and this is the way that we would solve it." It didn't all happen the day after Google Docs. It took like 10, 15, 20 years for people to invent all that stuff, and work out that you could do that with this. And so all of that is like, the way of saying, well, yes, it is going to be quick, but actually, no, it will kind of take a while for people to work out how to completely change how their business works.

是的。我的意思是，这里有个关键点，那就是我不喜欢权威论证。我觉得你突然负责AI实验室并不能因此就赋予你……或者更准确地说，如果你要用权威论证的话，那它应该与所在领域相关。所以，我对达里奥（Dario）对未来6到12个月模型发展方向的看法很感兴趣。但我对他关于劳动力市场价值和比较优势的观点不太感兴趣。没错，也许他大学时学过这方面的课程，我也学过。所以，我对达里奥的言论需要保持一定的警惕。先不谈他是否在为部门争取资源这种阴谋论，我对此深表怀疑。（00:18:50）：这又回到了我关于平台变革的观点上。每次新技术出现，都会淘汰大量工作岗位。而这种自动化，无论是价格弹性，还是自动化本身所带来的便利，都能创造出大量新就业机会。回溯到19世纪，我们90%的人都是农民，主要担忧是庄稼是否会歉收，因为那样我们就会挨饿，甚至更糟。从那以后，我们不断自动化工作岗位，创造新就业机会。你总能预见到即将消失的岗位，却看不到新岗位的诞生，因为它们还不存在，而且听起来很荒谬。比如铁路工程师，铁路是什么？为什么要那么快？我们一次又一次地经历这个过程。这是任何经济学新生都会告诉你的。自19世纪以来，我们一次又一次地经历这个过程。（00:19:41）：每次经历这个过程，都会带来大量的摩擦性痛苦和失业，许多人失去工作，许多城镇衰落，整个过程很糟糕。但当我们走出低谷时，我们都变得更富有，不再担心庄稼歉收。这就是过去200年的发展历程。那么问题来了，这次会有什么不同呢？因为互联网淘汰了大量工作，个人电脑淘汰了大量工作。现在已经没有排字工、电话接线员、打字员了。互联网淘汰了大量工作。从历史角度看，这些被淘汰的工作大多是低质量的，而新工作则更优质，因为GDP持续增长。（00:20:19）：那么AI有所不同吗？对此有两种观点。一是认为这次速度更快。确实AI的普及速度比以往技术更快，但这主要是因为我们站在巨人的肩膀上。你不需要等所有人购买昂贵的硬件、手机或PC，也不需要等电信公司部署宽带。这些基础设施已经存在。所以ChatGPT能拥有9亿用户，因为互联网用户本就有9亿。在马克·安德森（Mark Andreessen）于1993或1994年推出Netscape时，全球只有5000万到1亿台PC。所以当时没有9亿用户。但关键是他不需要等待电话网络或微芯片。在此之前，你也不需要等待电力和大规模生产。所以你总是站在巨人的肩膀上。这种复合效应不断叠加。所以这次速度更快，但互联网当时也更快。（00:21:11）：我认为另一个观点是……
回到专业服务领域这个话题。看看推特上那些悲观论者，他们总说每家大公司明天就会买下ChatGPT，两周后就裁掉所有员工，这些人简直是哀悼者。这种悲观情绪的根源之一，是他们完全不了解世界运作的规律。这也是他们无法理解其他事物的起点所在。拿大企业的软件销售周期来说——你比我更清楚，这周期通常长达18个月。问题在于，企业销售周期比风险投资资助周期更长。完成一笔企业级交易所需的时间远超完成一轮融资所需的时间。这对航空、医疗等传统行业的转型尤其不利。

（00:21:57）：我知道人们不会直接把SAP系统拆掉换成X、Y、Z系统。或许三五十年后，整个系统会焕然一新，所有岗位都会被替代，但这需要两三年、四五十年时间。每个行业的转型步伐都不同，人们需要逐步探索：“用这个工具就能实现那个功能。”

（00:22:19）：我记得安德森·霍洛维茨投资的一家公司Frame.io，专注于视频剪辑与协作。但其核心技术早在五年甚至十年前就该诞生了。说到这，可能用谷歌文档为例不太合适，因为它依赖尖端网络技术。但如果你随机挑选10家在ChatGPT问世前一天创立的SaaS公司，有几家能追溯到过去15年的某个时间点？

（00:22:54）：延迟的原因在于，人们意识到：“原来这个行业存在这样的痛点，我们可以用这个方案解决。”这绝不是谷歌文档问世后一夜之间发生的。人们花了10年、15年、20年才发明这些技术，验证其可行性。所以说，是的，变革速度会很快，但实际上还需要相当长时间，让人们彻底改变商业运作模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your view is so comforting, because basically it's like, okay, this is a huge deal, but we've been through many transformations before, and it's going to be okay.
turns.zh: 你的观点真让人宽慰，因为基本上就是说，好吧，这确实是个大挑战，但我们以前也经历过多次变革，总会挺过去的。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Well, I have a slide towards the end of the presentation, which I know the title is something like, "This is going to be completely different from everything else, just like everything else." And then the next slide is an IBM ad from the '50s, which has got this sea of white men holding up in white shirts and ties, all holding up flood rules. And the slogan of the title of the ad is, it's an IBM ad, it says, "An IBM electronic calculator..." This before it was called a computer, "... it's an electronic calculator it's the size of a fridge." Is like having 150 extra engineers. How many people listening to this company list, like their company slogan is basically will give you 150 extra engineers? I mean, isn't that like the whole pitch of Claude Code? 150 expert engineers for free. Or not free, that's like a lot of money. And yeah, that's what I gave you. (00:24:18): And so yes, we keep going through this over and over and over again, just to kind of make that tangible. I mean, obviously we couldn't be doing this without the internet. So there's a slide in my presentation, which is, we could maybe talk about, but it's a slide of chart showing how many products are stocked in supermarkets in America since the '50s. And the point of the slide is to say that barcodes allowed supermarkets to stock way more stuff because they could keep track of it. But making that chart, I had to know there was a thing called the Food Marketing Institute. And I had to have found out that they published a number for how many scoots there were in supermarkets every year. And then I had to realize they've been around since the '50s. And if I could dug long enough, I might be able to make a whole time series, and I could make whole chart. (00:25:03): Now imagine doing that in 1994. First of all, you would have no idea that exists. You really need to go and find a library where they publish, and they publish that number. And that the numbers in that report, you'd have no idea. Then you need to find a library that had them. So you're going to spend like three days on the phone, and spend like $50 on long distance phone calls to find a library that has these. Or maybe you call the Food Marketing Institute and they say, "We'll sell them to you for $500 each." So then you're going to get on, maybe you live in New York, or someone that has this. And two weeks later you've got the chart and you look at it. And then the other side of this is the life of an analyst is you spend all day making a chart and you look at it and go, "Oh, that's not really interesting." So you spend two weeks to make the chart and then you look at it and go, "Yeah, I'm not going to use that." (00:25:47): And for me, this was like two hours in Google. And so we forget how big a deal the internet was. That's a long way of saying it. But we forget we've had these absolutely enormous changes, and then we don't see it, because it's like that's the world the world's always been.
turns.zh: 嗯，我在演讲快结束时有一张幻灯片，标题大概是“这将与其他一切截然不同，正如其他一切一样”。下一张幻灯片是50年代的IBM广告，画面中是一群身着白衬衫、系着领带的白人男子，举着防洪规则的牌子。广告标语写着“IBM电子计算器……它比冰箱还小”。在那时它还没被称为计算机。“……它是一台电子计算器，尺寸和冰箱差不多。”就好像多了150名额外工程师似的。有多少听众听过这样的公司口号？我的意思是，克劳德·科德（Claude Code）的整个主张不就是免费提供150名专家工程师吗？或者说不免费，但那也是一大笔钱。反正我就是这么跟你们说的。（00:24:18）所以没错，我们一次又一次地反复探讨这些问题，就是为了让它更直观。显然，没有互联网我们根本无法做到这一点。演讲中有一张幻灯片，我们或许可以谈谈，但那是展示自50年代以来美国超市库存产品数量的图表。幻灯片的重点在于条形码让超市能够库存更多商品，因为他们能追踪库存情况。但制作这张图表时，我必须知道有个叫“食品营销协会”（Food Marketing Institute）的机构。我得查到他们每年发布的超市库存数量报告。然后我还得发现这个机构自50年代就存在了。如果我能深入挖掘，也许能构建出完整的时间序列和图表。（00:25:03）现在想象一下1994年做这件事的情景。首先，你根本不知道有这么个机构存在。你得去找个有该报告出版的图书馆，而这些报告的数据你一无所知。然后你还得找到存有这些资料的图书馆。这意味着你得花三天时间打电话，花50美元长途话费才能找到有这些资料的图书馆。或者你打电话给食品营销协会，他们可能会说每份报告500美元。所以你可能得去纽约，或者找其他有这些资料的人。两周后你拿到图表，看看后发现根本不感兴趣。对我来说，这只需要在谷歌上花两个小时。可见我们忘记了互联网带来的巨大变革。这话说得有点冗长，但我们忘记了自己经历过如此巨大的变革，却视而不见，因为这世界本就一直如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's different potentially this time, just even what your quote is, it's different, everything's going to change just like last time, the big difference obviously is AGI might emerge, and super intelligence. Does the work of humans can do a lot of this stuff for us, can actually replace jobs? Just like thoughts on that element of this transformation we're going through.
turns.zh: 这一次可能会有什么不同？单看你提到的引述内容，情况就有所不同。一切都将像上次一样发生巨变，显著的差异在于人工智能（AGI）或许会崛起，带来超级智能的到来。人类的工作能否替代大部分此类任务，进而取代大量就业岗位？关于我们正在经历的这场变革，您对这一层面有何见解？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I don't know. This is one of the ways I've struggled to write about AI is like certainly in 2023, early '24, all the questions were questions you could have asked in December 2022. And the questions didn't really change. And the strategies didn't really change. And I think the AGI question is kind of the same. I mean, the thing that the observation one can make, we have no theory of what human intelligence is, we have no theory of why these models work so well, we have no theory of how much better they will get. So we're all just kind of vibes forecasting as to what will happen. And then you can have like the 20 AM doped out philosophy students talking about, "Hey man, is this consciousness?" "Maybe we aren't conscious either. We just think we are." "Yeah, great. Thank you." (00:27:10): I think the one thing one can observe today is we have no idea. We don't know. We can guess, but we don't really know where this is going to end up. What I think you can say today is that there's a lot of kind of redefinition of terms. So I think a quote I used in my presentation late last year was an AI scientist called Larry Tesla who said AI is whatever machines can't do yet, because once machines can do it, people say, "Well, that's your software." And so certainly, I mean, I did do a poll on social media every now and then asking, "Is machine learning still AI?" Because I've certainly heard people say, "Well, that's not AI. That's just image recognition" "That's not AI. That's just sentiment analysis." So AI, it's a bit like the word technology. It's like if it's new, then it's technology. But in the '60s airline, jet airlines is the technology. Now a jet airline isn't tech. (00:27:57): And so there's a sort of sense of AI is like a moving target, is whatever just started working. And I think the point here is now clearly you can see people redefining AGI to mean the stuff that works now. (00:28:09): So is AEI, what's the definition now? It's like it can do a certain percentage of economically valuable work. Well, that's a very different thing too. It has a soul and it's fucking alive. Because a database could do that. Like an IBM mainframe in 1975 could do a meaningful percentage of economically valuable work that was previously done by people. And it turned out there was a whole bunch of other stuff that it couldn't do that we didn't do then, we didn't know existed. So there's a lot of creative redefinition here. Superintelligence, I'm not sure, is superintelligence more than AGI or less than AGI? Because last year I thought superintelligence was like really good, but not as good, not actual AGI. And now it's like, "Oh no, no, we've already got AGI, but superintelligence, that's really hard." (00:28:52): It's funny, I was having an argument on Hacker News this morning, you remember the argument, which is never a good use of time, but you remember the argument of like people would argue about whether crypto is blockchain, or whether blockchain is crypto. There isn't a right answer to that. Let's just be sure. It's important to understand what you mean when you say that, but there isn't like a correct answer to this. Are we going to get to something that has human level intelligence? We don't know. I don't think we have any way of answering that question. Maybe, maybe not. You can make arguments either way. Meantime, in the meanwhile, we've got this thing that's clearly kind of a completely transformative technology. And maybe the serious point here is like you don't have to believe, even if the model stopped it getting better tomorrow. If this is it and we hit a brick wall tomorrow, this is an incredibly useful technology that's going to change your world and get rolled out over the next 10 years. So you don't have to believe in any of that stuff to believe that this is a giant deal.
turns.zh:
我不知道。这是我在写人工智能相关内容时遇到的难题之一——比如说，在2023年初到2024年初，所有问题都是2022年12月就能提出的那些。这些问题本质上并未发生变化，相关策略也未曾更新。我认为通用人工智能（AGI）的问题也差不多。我们可以观察到，人类智能究竟是什么？为什么这些模型效果如此出色？它们还能提升到何种程度？对此我们都只是在凭直觉预测。然后你会听到早上8点的哲学系学生在讨论：“嘿，伙计，这算意识吗？” “也许我们根本没有意识，只是自以为有。” “嗯，不错，谢谢。”  
（00:27:10）：我认为如今我们能观察到的一点是，我们毫无头绪。我们不知道。我们可以猜测，但确实不知道最终会走向何方。今天可以说的是，术语正在被重新定义。去年我在演讲中引用了人工智能科学家拉里·特斯拉的话，他说人工智能就是机器目前还做不到的事情，因为一旦机器能做到了，人们就会说：“这不过是软件罢了。” 确实，我偶尔会在社交媒体上发起民意调查，询问“机器学习还是人工智能吗？” 因为我确实听到有人说：“这不是人工智能，只是图像识别。”  “这不是人工智能，只是情感分析。” 所以人工智能有点像技术这个词。只要是新的，就是技术。但在60年代，航空公司就是技术。如今的喷气式飞机公司却不再算技术了。  
（00:27:57）：所以人工智能就像一个移动的靶子，就是刚开始能运作的东西。我认为关键在于，现在人们显然把AGI重新定义为当前能运作的东西。  
（00:28:09）：那么AEI，现在的定义是什么？就是能完成一定比例的经济有价值工作。嗯，这又是个截然不同的概念。它有灵魂，它他妈的活着。因为数据库也能做到。1975年的IBM大型机就能完成人类过去做过的经济有价值工作的合理比例。结果发现还有一堆它做不到的功能，而我们当时并不知道这些功能的存在。所以这里有很多创造性的重新定义。超智能，我不确定，它是比AGI更强还是弱？因为去年我认为超智能很不错，但不如真正的AGI。现在人们又说：“哦，不不，我们已经有AGI了，但超智能太难了。” 
（00:28:52）：挺有意思的，我今天早上在Hacker News上争论这个事儿，你应该记得那场争论——根本不值得花时间，但你肯定记得。就是关于加密货币是不是区块链，或者区块链是不是加密货币。没有正确答案。关键是理解你说这话的意思，但这问题没有标准答案。我们能达到人类级别的智能吗？不知道。我觉得我们没法回答这个问题。也许能，也许不能。两边都能说得通。与此同时，我们拥有一项显然彻底变革技术的东西。或许关键在于，即便模型明天就停止提升，你也不必因此怀疑。只要……
即便明天我们遇到重重阻碍，这项极具革命性的技术仍将彻底改变我们的生活，并在未来十年内全面普及。因此，即便你不认同这些观点，也不得不承认这是一项意义非凡的突破。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that's definitely changed, I had your former boss, Mark Andreessen on the podcast, and we didn't actually talk about this during the conversation, and he brought it up before we started recording and I never got to it, is he had this insight that the opportunity set for companies now is so much larger. We used to have no trillion-dollar companies, now we're going to have dozens of trillion-dollar companies. Just like the size companies can grow to are going up so much, and valuations also go up along with that. And his point is just people haven't really grokked just how large companies can get now. Everyone's hitting a hundred million AR in five months, six months. Just thoughts on that.
turns.zh: 有一件事确实发生了变化。我在播客上邀请了你的前老板马克·安德森（Mark Andreessen），但我们在对话中并未深入探讨这个话题。他在录制前提到了这一点，而我当时没来得及深入讨论。他认为，如今企业的机遇规模要大得多。过去我们没有万亿美元市值的公司，而现在将有数十家这样的巨头出现。企业能发展到的大小规模正在显著提升，估值也随之水涨船高。他指出的问题是，人们尚未充分认识到当下企业能发展到何种规模。如今很多公司能在五六个月内就实现月营收1亿美元。这只是我对此的一些思考。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, this was his whole software's eating the world thesis from 15 years ago, whenever it was. Yeah. The TAM, it gets progressively bigger, because you can address larger and larger parts of the economy. And so if you think about the classic platform ship framing that mainframes are, I think peak mainframe install base was something like 70, 80,000 units. I mean, slightly fuzzy term, what exactly is a mainframe, and at what point does it become two mainframes as one. But something like that, that order of magnitude. And then when the internet kicks off, there are, as I said, 50 to 100 million PCs on earth, maybe. Today there are something over a billion, one to one and a half billion, but obviously a lot of those are corporate. Like seven, 800 million consumer PCs in the world. There's about five and a half, six billion smartphones in the world, which is why you can have 900 million weekly active users on ChatGPT. (00:31:16): And so there was this narrative five years ago of like, "Well, we've run out of people. So the next thing can't be in order of magnitude bigger." Which was true up to a point, but that was the wrong model, because clearly what's happening now as you're moving in another direction, is you're just branching out and automating big news weights of the economy. (00:31:33): Now, back to your job point, you could argue, well, we're just going to replace all the people with AI and all the money will go to Sam Altman. And Mark can buy himself another Gulfstream, add to the fleet. I think the other answer, it's back to the lump of labor fallacy, and the last 200 years, that each of these technologies removes a bunch of jobs, creates a bunch of new jobs, creates a bunch of new value, unlocks prosperity for all of us, and that's painful as you go through it, but it always creates more value. And so here you could certainly make an analog to... The useful analog to the electricity industry is just saying how that electricity became part of absolutely everything. And software has been kind of slowly working its way out. Another would be electricity in factories, and then electricity sort of slowly spreads out. And so that would be the point again, that it slowly spreads out to do more and more things. And so more and more value and a bigger and bigger contribution to the economy. (00:32:36): Also, of course, disappears inside things. And the other side, the point of my capital section in the presentation is there's this quote from Sam Altman where he said, "We're going to be selling AI intelligence on a meter like water or electricity." And you look at this and think, "My dear sweet child, you need me to explain the margin structure of the utility industry to you." Because guess what? When you watch television, the TV company isn't paying a percentage of your monthly bill to the electricity company. When you wash your clothes, Bosch isn't paying a percentage of the price of the washing machine. And clearly, this is like the much more specific tactical question at the moment, is, do we even end up with three giant models or does it become hundreds of models and open models and local models and so on? (00:33:26): And even if we do end up with, say, pick a number, three to six to 10 giant foundation models that cost hundreds of billions of dollars a year, fine, do they get all the value from that? Now, I started my career as a telecom analyst, and so still pay attention to it a bit. Global mobile industry has revenue of about a trillion dollars a year, maybe a bit more now. And it spends about $200 billion a year on CapEx every year. Total telecoms is about 300. Mobile is about 200. It's about 15, 20% of revenue every year. And if you look at a chart of mobile data consumption, it's an exponential curve, like perfect curve going spread up. And the number now, I think it's about 1,500 to 2,000 times what it was in 2010 globally. (00:34:11): And the stocks have gone nowhere in 25 years, because it's an X gross low margin commodity utility, where they're selling this objectively amazing piece of global technology infrastructure that has enormous complexity and enormous sophistication, but all the cool stuff is made by you. It's made by the people listening to this podcast. It's made by somebody else. This was that kind of pivotal moment where the telcos thought that they would do all the stuff that you did on your iPhone. And not only do they not do it, but Apple doesn't do it either. (00:34:47): It's all further up stack. And so this is the elemental question right now around foundation models is, does the model do the whole thing? Do you just go to the chatbot and get the chatbot to do the whole thing? Can the model companies keep building these like Claude for X, Claude for Y things, which to me look very much like what you see if you hit file new in Excel. It's like the tablets, but all of those are actually billion-dollar companies as well. And if not, no, does it all have to be "apps"? Whatever app means. And if it all has to be apps who builds those, well, they can't all get built by the model labs, just as they didn't all get built by Microsoft. And so if they're all built by other companies, does their notion models have leverage up the stack the way Windows did? Or is this more like AWS where, if you're, I don't know, an engineering company or a law firm buying a piece of software, you don't care which cloud it runs on? (00:35:37): And you don't have to standardize on AWS because that's where all the software is. And the developers all standardize on AWS because all the customers use AWS. That's not how it works. That's how Windows or iOS works, but that's not how AWS works. And so it does sort of seem to me that if the chatbot isn't the UX, and it needs to be apps, and the model companies aren't going to build that, and the models themselves are basically commodities, at least as you can see them as users, then why would the model companies have pricing power? And wouldn't all the value be further up the stack? Aren't you basically, have you got like three to six companies selling a commodity at marginal cost? Now, obviously the semi-analyst guys are like, "No, no, no, no, no. There's going to be infinite pricing power forever." I'm sorry, I'm exaggerating. (00:36:18): But I think you have to really important to draw a distinction between where are we now, where you have radical price disequilibrium, and you've got these, what's the guy, the OpenClaw guy spent one and a half million dollars on token this last month. But that's somebody getting like a 50 grand mobile data built in 2010. That's temporary. What is the steady state equilibrium point where all of these lines on the chart kind of get lined up, and we don't have this kind of weird, crazy stuff going on? And then will you have pricing power, or have you got like three or four or five companies kind of all selling the same thing? And so then you should have a pricing price. You should have lower pricing and lower margins, and the value you've got stack.
turns.zh:
是啊。我是说，他15年前提出的"软件吞噬世界"的论点至今仍适用。TAM（总可寻址市场）会不断扩大，因为你能覆盖的经济领域越来越广。想想经典的平台船理论——主机系统最多也就7万到8万台。主机的定义有点模糊，什么时候两个主机算一个？但数量级是差不多的。互联网兴起后，全球PC数量达到5千万到1亿台。如今智能手机数量超过60亿台，这也是ChatGPT能吸引9亿周活用户的原因。（00:31:16）五年前有人说"用户群体已经饱和，下一个增长点不可能再翻倍"。这在一定程度上是正确的，但这种思维模式是错误的。因为当技术向新方向发展时，你只需不断扩展触角，自动化经济中的关键环节。（00:31:33）回到就业问题，你可能会说"用AI取代所有人类，钱全进山姆·奥尔特曼口袋"。但正确的解读应基于劳动力谬论。过去200年，每项技术都淘汰大量岗位，同时创造新就业机会、释放价值，促进社会繁荣。转型固然痛苦，但最终价值会增长。电力行业的类比很贴切——电力逐渐渗透各领域。软件也正以同样的逻辑扩展应用场景，创造更大价值。（00:32:36）当然，价值也会内化于产品。幻灯片中引用山姆·奥尔特曼的话"AI智能将像水电一样按量出售"，这话听起来天真。试想电视用户不用向电力公司分摊费用，博世洗衣机也不需向电力公司支付分成。关键问题是，未来会出现三个巨型模型，还是数百个开放模型、本地模型？（00:33:26）即便出现3-10个年营收数百亿美元的巨型模型，收益能全部归它们吗？我曾是电信分析师，对行业仍有关注。全球移动产业年营收约1万亿美元，如今支出约2000亿美元。
每年的资本支出（CapEx）。整个电信行业约为300亿美元，其中移动业务约200亿美元。这些支出占年度收入的15%至20%。如果你看一下移动数据消费的图表，会发现这是一条指数曲线——就像完美向上延伸的曲线。目前全球移动数据消费量比2010年增长了约1500至2000倍。  
（00:34:11）：过去25年里，电信股毫无进展，因为它们是低毛利的商品公用事业。尽管出售的是客观上令人惊叹的全球技术基础设施，具有极高的复杂性和精密度，但所有核心技术都由他人创造——比如听这个播客的听众们。  
（00:34:47）：这正是关键问题所在：基础模型能否完成整个任务？你是否只需使用聊天机器人来完成所有工作？模型公司能否持续开发类似Claude for X、Claude for Y的工具？在我看来，这些工具就像Excel中新建文件时的模板。就像平板电脑，但这些公司也都价值数十亿美元。若不然，是否一切都必须通过“应用程序”实现？但应用程序又意味着什么？若一切都必须通过应用程序实现，谁来开发这些应用？正如微软未能独自完成所有开发任务一样，其他公司也无法单独完成。  
（00:35:37）：当所有应用都由其他公司开发时，模型技术能否像Windows那样向上层级渗透？还是更像AWS那样——工程公司或律师事务所购买软件时并不在意其运行的云平台？AWS之所以成功，是因为所有客户都使用该平台，开发者也因此统一标准。
