They're replacing Chromebooks with Google Books, and they've got a new Android intelligence powered by Gemini that will roll out to the five people who bought a Pixel phone. You don't work for Google.
turns.zh: 嗯，不，他们上周就发布了，这恰恰说明我们对安卓和iPhone的关注度有多高了。谷歌上周搞了场大发布。他们要用谷歌图书取代Chromebooks，还推出了由Gemini驱动的新安卓智能功能，先在五个买了Pixel手机的用户中试用。你又不在谷歌工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I want to go in a slightly different direction. Something that I'm curious if you're following is just the anti-AI sentiment that feels like is growing. It feels like if you've seen these surveys, AI is less popular than ICE, people are trying to stop data centers from being built. I think Eric Schmidt just did a commencement speech and people were booing him every time he mentioned AI. Just like, "What do you think is going on? Where do you think this goes over time?"
turns.zh: 是啊。我想聊点别的。我很好奇你是否关注到反人工智能的情绪似乎在升温。比如你看那些调查，人工智能的支持率比ICE（移民与海关执法局）还低，还有人反对建数据中心。我记得埃里克·施密特刚做完毕业典礼演讲，每次提到人工智能都会被喝倒彩。就想问问，你怎么看？你觉得这股反感会持续下去吗？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: It's interesting. And it's a big sort of fuzzy mass of different stuff, I think. There is tangible, like my electricity bill went up, which applies actually in a very small number of places, objectively, but it did, and this is a question. The water thing is weird because it's just completely fake. And I should explain what I mean here. Data centers use water for cooling. It's mostly closed loop, but the number of data centers relative to the total amount of water use in the USA is tiny. (00:49:13): I actually went and dug into this that the Livermore lab did a study at the end of 2024 where they estimated US data center water consumption. And it came out at about 0.017% of US water consumption. Now, obviously if you live in a small town and you've got one well and they capped the well and gave all the water to the data center, then you're really pissed off. But that's a planning problem. That's not a data center problem. In generality, yes, this is data centers of what, like 5% of US energy, and might grow at 1% a year for the next five years, one percentage point a year, but the water stuff is just nonsense. (00:49:51): And then you get into more tangible like, well, what is happening with this? Is it taking jobs away? Where you can watch a bunch of three-hour podcasts of economists talking to each other and the main answer is we really don't know yet. There's a bunch of charts that kind of say yes and a bunch of charts that kind of say no. And clearly there's a slowdown in employment of 18 to 24 year olds, but that seems to be the same for people who do and don't have degrees, and the same for people in fields that look exposed to AI and feels that they look exposed to AI. (00:50:25): So there's a lot of econometric argument about this. And I mean, there's a broader point here, in fact, which is a different point here, that we have very little data on what's going on in AI, from anyone. The model labs don't tell us anything. They don't give us any meaningful usage information. They give us these weird studies of people, how many people use this for this and that. They don't give us a daily active use number. We do not have a daily active user number for us for ChatGPT. It's crazy. And all the data comes from academic economists trying to back stuff out of BLS surveys. Or consultancies and marketing agencies like spending a whole bunch of money to survey 20,000 people and saying, "What are you doing with this stuff?" (00:51:05): We don't have good data on what's going on and how many people are really using this, but to the employment question, hence there's a lot of people looking through all the stuff that the US census collects and trying to work out, "Well, where can we see this? Can we see productivity? What could we see?" And the answer right now I think is there's no clear consensus that we're seeing an impact on jobs, but of course, politically that doesn't matter. If you're a student and you can't get a job, and that clearly is an issue, whether it's because of AI or whether it's because of Trump and tariffs is a different question. (00:51:32): Then you get niche things like people who draw book covers for young adult romance novels are very upset that now you can get a picture of a naked woman on back of a dragon flying through a volcano without paying them. I'm sorry, I'm being deliberately unkind, but there's a little... And particularly novelists, people who write eBooks, there's a huge culture war over whether it's okay to use AI. There's this whole sort of AI slop question, and obviously you show the number that like 30, 40% of your podcasts are generated by AI. There's a big fuzzy massive questions. (00:52:06): Some of this, I think it's a little bit like the backlash we had around social, but much more compressed. And like social, some of the backlash around social was true, and some of it was sort of true, and some of it wasn't. Always like exemplified in the whole Facebook sells your data thing, which is just, A, not true, and B, the people who believe it are absolutely adamant that of course it's true, and you're obviously a lunatic for suggesting otherwise. It's like the line from Jonathan Swift that you can't reason somebody out of an idea that went reasonably to. (00:52:38): So you get this kind of wide, it was a long answer question, but you've got this wide spread of ideas just as you kind of did with social. There's like 20 different things, some of which are really real, and some of which are really not real. And a lot of which are kind of a fuzzy mess in the middle. All of which means that meanwhile, you've got Trump saying he wants a new executive order on dangerous models, which I actually don't think is the thing that drives the backlash. The worrying about myth or cyber, I don't feel like that's a main street America conversation, but that's the thing that got Trump interested in this stuff again.
turns.zh:
真有意思。这简直是一团混乱的复杂局面。我觉得里面有不少实际问题，但也有很多虚假信息。比如电费上涨这事，虽然只影响少数地区，但确实发生了。水资源问题更是荒谬——数据中心用水降温确实需要大量水资源，但相较于美国总用水量而言，数据中心用水占比微不足道。

（00:49:13）我特意查阅了相关资料。利弗莫尔国家实验室在2024年底发布的研究报告估算，美国数据中心用水量仅占全国总用水量的0.017%。当然，如果你住在小镇，水井被封锁后全被数据中心占用，那肯定会愤愤不平。但这属于规划问题，跟数据中心无关。总体而言，数据中心消耗的能源约占美国总能耗的5%，而且未来五年每年增长1%。但水资源问题纯属无稽之谈。

（00:49:51）再说就业问题——有三小时的播客节目，经济学家们互相讨论，但主要结论是尚无定论。各种数据图表有的说有影响，有的说没有。18到24岁年轻人失业率确实下降，但受教育程度高低、AI相关领域人员就业情况差异等因素影响尚不明确。

（00:50:25）经济学界对此争论不休。更深层问题是，我们对AI领域缺乏可靠数据。模型实验室从不透露有效数据，仅提供用户使用量统计。ChatGPT的日活用户数至今未公布。疯狂的是，相关数据多来自学术经济学家通过BLS调查推测，或者是咨询公司花大钱调查2万人后得出结论。

（00:51:05）就业问题缺乏有效数据，人们只能从美国人口普查数据中挖掘线索，比如生产率变化等。目前尚无共识证明AI对就业有显著影响，但政治层面无需在意。如果学生找不到工作，无论是AI还是特朗普关税导致的贸易战，都是现实问题。

（00:51:32）还有特定群体如青少年言情小说封面设计师的困境——现在随便一张龙飞凤舞的裸女图片就能用于封面，而设计师却得不到报酬。抱歉，我故意说得刻薄些，但确实存在文化冲突。尤其在电子书领域，AI是否被合理使用引发激烈争论。
你们30%到40%的播客内容是由人工智能生成的。这背后存在着一个巨大而混乱的争议。（00:52:06）：我觉得这有点像我们在社交媒体领域遇到的反弹，但这次反弹来得更猛烈。就像社交媒体的反弹一样，有些批评是合理的，有些则言过其实。以Facebook出售用户数据的传闻为例，这个说法首先就是不实的。而相信这说法的人又坚信它千真万确，认为提出相反观点的人简直就是疯子。正如乔纳森·斯威夫特所说："对于一个合乎情理的观点，永远无法用理性说服那些固执己见的人。"（00:52:38）：所以我们面对的是一个复杂的局面，这是一个很长的回答，但里面充斥着各种各样的观点。有些观点确有其事，有些则纯属虚构，还有很多介于两者之间模糊不清的灰色地带。与此同时，特朗普声称要针对危险算法发布新行政令，但我认为这并非引发反弹的核心原因。人们对网络安全和虚假信息的担忧，似乎并非美国主流社会关注的焦点，但正是这些担忧再次激发了特朗普对此事的兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me go kind of in a tangential direction. Something that I like to ask folks that have kids that come on the podcast, especially people that are thinking so deeply about where things are going, knowing what you know about just where the world is heading, what AI is going to do to the future, how are you changing the way you raise your kids? Just what are you teaching them differently potentially that might help them in the future?
turns.zh: 容我稍微偏个题。我特别喜欢问那些有孩子、做客播客节目的嘉宾，尤其是那些对未来趋势深思熟虑的人——鉴于你对世界走向的了解，以及人工智能将如何改变未来，请问你如何改变养育孩子的方式？你是否在教给他们一些可能对未来有益的不同理念？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I don't know. I think there's a curve here in that if you've got kids who are going onto the job market in the next year or two, then everything is up in the air and no one knows how this is going to work. If you've got kids who are going onto the job market in like five years, then who knows? But staff will have settled down a lot by then in probably unpredictable ways. So, I could be a lot more worried if I had a 21-year-old. I don't, I've got a kid in his sort of early teens. Those questions vary. (00:54:05): Then you've got a lot of the questions that were the same before ChatGPT around the collapse of gatekeepers, "Should you really believe what that influence on TikTok says?" "And where exactly you're getting your understanding of what's going on in Israel?" And all of those kinds of social media, internety, media consumption kinds of questions. (00:54:32): I don't know. There are people who are super, super intentional about every minute of their child's life. I'm not. I kind of recall the George Carlin line that anyone who drives faster than you is a maniac and anyone who drives slower is an idiot, and that certainly applies to parenting. And everybody thinks they're somewhere in the middle, but I don't have a deeply systematic and widespread and coherent plan for, "This is what my child is going to be doing in three, six, 12, 18 months time." I'd settle for him not breaking his Chromebook again.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我觉得这里面有个曲线：如果你的孩子将在未来一两年内进入职场，那么一切都尚未明朗，没有人知道这会如何发展。但如果你的孩子要在五年后进入职场，谁知道呢？到那时，社会规范很可能已经发生了难以预料的变化。所以，如果我有个21岁的孩子，我会担忧得多。但我现在有个十岁出头的孩子。这些问题因人而异。（00:54:05）：然后还有很多在ChatGPT出现之前就存在的问题，比如关于网关守护者的崩塌，"你真的应该相信TikTok上的那些影响力人物所说的话吗？" "你从哪里获得对以色列局势的准确理解？" 以及所有这类社交媒体、互联网和媒体消费相关的问题。（00:54:32）：我不知道。有些人对孩子生活的每一分钟都操控得极其细致。我不是这样。我总会想起乔治·卡林的那句话："开车比你快的人都是疯子，开车比你慢的人都是白痴。"这句话放在育儿上也适用，每个人都觉得自己处于中间位置，但我没有一个系统化、全面且连贯的计划，"我的孩子三个月、六个月、十二个月、十八个月后会做什么。"我只要他别再把Chromebook弄坏就行了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that you're just general vibe is, "It's going to be okay, guys. It's going to be okay."
turns.zh: 我喜欢你传递出的那种整体氛围："没事的，朋友们。一切都会好起来的。"

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Yeah. I don't know, maybe this is because I'm British and we haven't had political violence in 500 years, and I think maybe if I came from Iran, I'd have a different attitude to being calm about the future. I think there's a layer of like, yes, this will change a bunch of stuff and we'll need to worry about it, but that's kind of a constant, we've always had that. I remember in the whole wave of panic around social media, I dug up, so were a whole bunch of books in the late '70s about databases. There was a whole panic about databases. And again, half of it was true. If everybody's police records, and if all police records and all government records are online, then that's different. If you think about, for example, the deep fake needs issue, for example, there's like a dumb reaction to this, which is to say, "Haven't you heard of Photoshop?" Which is true, but a 15-year-old kid couldn't use Photoshop to make hardcore pornographic news of every girl in their high school and send them to the whole school in one afternoon.
turns.zh: 是啊。我不知道，也许是因为我是英国人，我们500年来都没有经历过政治暴力吧。我觉得如果我来自伊朗，我对未来的态度可能会不同。我觉得有层意思是，"是的，这会改变很多东西，我们需要担忧，但这其实是常态，我们一直如此。"我记得在社交媒体引发恐慌的那波浪潮中，我翻出了70年代末一堆关于数据库的书。当时人们对数据库也曾恐慌过。但其中一半是真的。如果所有人的警方记录、所有政府记录都上网，那确实不同了。再比如，关于深度伪造技术的问题，人们对此的反应往往很愚蠢，比如"你没听说过Photoshop吗？"这倒是事实，但一个15岁的孩子不可能用Photoshop制作高中女生硬核色情新闻，并在一天内发送给全校学生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And tournament the video.
turns.zh: 还有剪辑视频。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Exactly. Even more. Yeah, even more. And now they can. So, that is different. It's kind of like the challenge of social. The thing people would say in the '90s is it's great. You can read the only gay kid in your village, and you can find other gay people, and you can find your tribe. And guess what? It turned out you could also be the only Nazi in your village, or the only pedophile in your village, or somebody wanted to look at child porn. Yeah, now you can find the other people who like looking at child porn and they'll tell you it's great. So oops, we connected everybody. And unfortunately, that meant we connected all the bad people, and all of our own worst instincts, and every problem in society. And so that will happen again with AI. Deep fake news are like the obvious thing we can see now. There will be a whole bunch more of this stuff. (00:57:11): But there's also, and something a kind of technical audience should know about, do you know about the post office scandal in the UK?
turns.zh: 没错。甚至更甚。是啊，甚至更甚。现在他们做到了。所以，这就是不同之处。这有点像社交媒体带来的挑战。90年代人们会说，这太棒了。你能读到村里唯一的同性恋者，还能找到其他同性恋者，找到自己的同类。猜猜怎么着？结果你还能成为村里唯一的纳粹分子，唯一的恋童癖，或者某个想看儿童色情的人。是啊，现在你能找到其他喜欢看儿童色情的人，他们还会告诉你这很棒。所以，哎呀，我们把所有人都连在了一起。不幸的是，这意味着我们把所有坏人也连在了一起，还有我们自己最糟糕的本能，以及社会上的各种问题。人工智能也会重蹈覆辙。深度换脸新闻就是我们现在能看到的明显例子。未来还会有更多类似的案例。（00:57:11）：但还有一点，技术爱好者应该了解的，你知道英国的邮局丑闻吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nope.
turns.zh: 不知道。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Okay. So sidebar here. So in the UK, post offices are mostly franchises run by small business people. So they're run by pharmacies classically, very often Indian, Indian immigrants, second generation Indian people. And the post office 15 years ago rolled out a new point to sell computer system. So they have a separate counter in the back that's a post office. And so the post office rolled out this new computer system built by them by Fujitsu that had a bunch of bugs in it that showed shortfalls in cash. And the post office looks at this and says, "Aha, we knew these people were stealing from us." Hundreds of people get prison, bunch of suicides, bunch of bankruptcies, people lose their homes. (00:57:56): Meanwhile, people from the post office and people from Fujitsu are going to court and swearing there's no bugs in the system and nobody else has had this problem. This is 1970s technology. That's really the point, that every wave of technology comes with ways that you can ruin people's lives either deliberately or by accident. The whole thing of Chinese mass surveillance is deliberate. Maybe people should go to prison, maybe not, but we have this with every technology. We have a bunch of ways that you can ruin people's lives, and you have to be conscious of that and also kind of not panic about it.
turns.zh: 好的。说点题外话。在英国，邮局大多是小商人经营的特许经营店。通常由药店经营，经营者多是印度人，印度移民，或者第二代印度人。15年前，邮局推出了一个新的电脑系统销售点。所以在后台有一个单独的柜台，那里是邮局。邮局推出了这个由富士通开发的新电脑系统，系统存在大量漏洞，导致现金短缺。邮局查出问题后声称：“啊，我们早就知道这些人在偷我们的钱。”数百人入狱，多人自杀，多人破产，人们失去了家园。（00:57:56）：与此同时，邮局和富士通的人在法庭上发誓系统没有漏洞，没有其他人遇到过这个问题。这是20世纪70年代的技术。这才是关键，每一波技术浪潮都会带来可以故意或意外毁掉人们生活的方式。中国的全民监控是故意为之。也许这些人应该入狱，也许不应该，但每项技术都会带来这种风险。我们有很多方法可以毁掉人们的生活，对此我们必须保持清醒，也不必因此恐慌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So maybe following that the right and coming back to the kids thing and the jobs thing, is there a job you are steering your kid away from? And is there a job you kind of think you want to steer them towards?
turns.zh: 那么，也许接下来谈谈右派观点，再回归到孩子和工作的话题，有没有你想让孩子远离的职业？有没有你觉得应该让孩子向往的职业？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I don't know about that. It's probably a little bit early yet. He's not quite at the like, "I want to be a fireman stage," but...
turns.zh: 我现在还不太清楚。现在他还没到想当消防员的阶段，不过……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That might be a great job.
turns.zh: 那或许是个很棒的工作。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Yeah. And certainly if I look at my career, I started as an equity analyst, and then I went and worked in an industry, and then I was a consultant. The days when you kind of knew what your career was going to be over, there were sickly some people were like, you want to be an architect, you want to be a software engineer, you want to be X or Y. I don't know. I think the only kind of thinking I have here is that you slowly work out, there's a bunch of skills that you have, and there's a bunch of jobs that makes you good at, and then there's a bunch of stuff that people will pay you for. And you want to get at least two of those, and preferably all three.
turns.zh: 是啊。要说我的职业生涯，我最初是做股票分析师的，后来转行进入某个行业，再后来又做了咨询顾问。过去那种能预知自己职业发展轨迹的日子已经一去不复返了——那时人们会说：你想当建筑师？软件工程师？还是干别的工作？我也不知道。我现在唯一的想法是，你得慢慢摸索清楚自己拥有哪些技能，擅长哪些工作领域，然后找出能为之付费的岗位。至少要满足其中两项，最好是全部三项。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So zooming out a little bit, let me ask you a Meta question. What's a question about AI that you think nobody's asking yet, or not enough people are asking that we should be asking ourselves?
turns.zh: 好的。退后一步，问你一个元问题吧。关于人工智能，有什么问题是你觉得目前还没人问，或者问的人太少，而我们应该自问自答的？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Sure. I mean, we talked about value capture. Obviously this is a whole, everyone is asking like, I'm not sure how many people are asking whether model labs have pricing power. I think a lot of people are just presuming that the situation today will continue, or that of course they will. So I think that's maybe a question that not enough people ask. (00:59:52): I think the question I pose towards the end of my presentation, which we talked about earlier, is like, what's the task and what's job? Or what is just the thing that becomes a button or make SKU versus what are people actually hiring you for? Is that kind of a useful way of thinking about this? And clearly there are going to be some jobs where no, that is just a task, and that job gets automated away. But there's a bunch where that kind of isn't the question. (01:00:15): The way I actually pulled that together at the end of the deck was a chart of a global recorded music revenue, which as you may know is kind of a U-shaped curve more or less. And so it's dropped by about half from 2000 to 2015 or so, and since then has come back to about 75% of the peak, adjusted for inflation. And the way that I look at this is to say, and that's driven by streaming. And I kind of looked at this and said, well, the first half of this chart is saying, what happens if I don't have to pay $15 to get a CD to get that track? And the second half of the chart is saying, what happens if $15 a month gets you all the music that there is? So it's kind of a completely different sort of question. And that's a way that you could look at Google, or the way you could look at Airbnb or all these kinds of companies. (01:01:03): Is it to begin with you do the old thing but more whether you need technology, you do the old thing, but more of it on the new place. So you put Flickable mobile, you print out Googles, and then you make new things that are only possible with a new thing. And then maybe you go a bit further and you kind of completely redefine the question and you make something that isn't that at all. Spotify is not an online music store. It's something else. And right now, those questions, you only even know what the question is after it's been asked and you've built a billion dollar thing that lots of people use because obviously Spotify look crazy, and people look crazy, and Airbnb look crazy. But that's, I think, the way to get at what this means, is you have to get past, we do the old stuff but more, and you have to get to what do you do that's different that's because of this. What has this change? What wasn't possible before? What gets unlocked as opposed to just doing the old thing but more of it?
turns.zh:
好的。我的意思是，我们之前讨论了价值捕获问题。显然，这是一个复杂的议题。很多人都在问，模型实验室是否具有定价权。我认为很多人只是假设现状会延续下去，或者理所当然地认为他们一定会有定价权。所以我觉得这或许是一个被忽视的问题。（00:59:52）：我在演讲结尾提出的那个问题，我们之前也讨论过，那就是任务和工作的区别。或者说，什么样的工作会成为按钮式操作，什么样的产品需要人力投入？这或许是一种有用的思考方式。显然，有些工作就是纯粹的任务性工作，会被自动化取代。但很多工作并非如此。

（01:00:15）：我在演示文稿结尾用了一张全球录音音乐收入图表，可能大家都知道，这张图大致呈U型曲线。从2000年到2015年左右，收入减少了大约一半，调整通货膨胀因素后，目前已恢复到峰值的75%。我认为这背后是流媒体的推动。我仔细分析后发现，上半部分的问题是，如果不必花15美元买CD获取那首歌曲会怎样？下半部分的问题是，如果每月15美元就能获取所有音乐会怎样？这完全是两个不同的问题。这也是我们观察谷歌、Airbnb等公司的方式。

（01:01:03）：最初可能只是在原有基础上做更多事，但后来需要技术支持。或者在新平台上做更多原有业务。比如推出Flickable移动应用，印制谷歌地图，再开发只有新技术才能实现的新产品。接下来可能更进一步，彻底重新定义问题，创造出与原有业务完全不同的事物。Spotify不是在线音乐商店，而是另类存在。现在这些问题，只有在提出后才知道答案，最终打造出数十亿美元规模、被广泛使用的平台，因为Spotify和Airbnb的发展令人惊叹。但我认为，要理解其意义，就必须突破“在原有基础上做更多事”的思维局限，转向“因技术变革而产生的全新可能性”：哪些事物因技术而诞生，哪些事物因技术而被解锁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Just to support this kind of general theme you have of it's like we don't know what is going to happen, this is unprecedented, if you're to zoom out a few years ago, maybe three years ago, four years ago, the last profession you think would be automated is engineering and coding. It's like, that feels like the hardest thing that's like, we're going to need people to build these things. Now it's like the most transformed role of any role. You went from writing all your codes to 0% of your code is AI.
turns.zh: 是的。为了支持你提到的这个总体论点——我们不知道未来会怎样，这是一次前所未有的变革。如果回看几年前，也许是三四年前，人们认为最不可能被自动化取代的职业是工程和编程。当时觉得这些是最难的工作，必须有人来开发这些产品。现在却成了变化最剧烈的行业。从完全手写代码到0%用AI编写代码，转变之大令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: It's almost like you didn't realize it was boring manual labor that could be automated. You thought it was something else. It's funny. I mean, I was looking at this, this whole, there's this sort of US government called data set called ONET or something like that, which tries to analyze every single job and then people try and kind of score it, and they try and say, "Well, this profession is X or Y percent exposed to AI, and AI can do Z percent of it today." I think this is just the most ridiculous bunch of diluted horseshit. And there's two reasons for this. The first reason is that this is, ironically, this is the logical systems problem, the expert system's problem. The problem with expert systems is, for anyone who doesn't know, you try to recognize a picture of a cat and so you start building up logical steps. (01:03:14): So you make an edge detector, and then you make a third detector, and you make an eye detector and you make an ear detector, and 15 years later you've got 700 steps and it doesn't work. (01:03:25): And this is what happens when you try and look at a profession and sort of break it down by which bits can be automated and which can't. You can't describe a profession like that. But anyway, we can't. You can't look at a senior partner at a law firm and say, "Well, 17% of their work could be automated." This is horseshit. You can't do that. (01:03:43): I think the other side of the fallacy though is to talk about taxi drivers. So, if we'd been having this conversation in 1997, it's like the Uber test. Imagine we're in 1997, what will be crushed by the internet? Well, newspapers will be fine because they'll save money on the printing bills. This is like a jake, but people said that. Newspaper, the internet will be great for newspapers. Their printing bills will get down. Well, yes, but no. But the other side is, well, obviously our taxi drivers, you couldn't automate that with the internet. It's got nothing to do with the internet. Maybe you'd have internet booking, but like, no, that's not going to change anything. And of course, it completely changes the whole thing. And so the example I saw the other day was things that won't be affected by AI personal trainers. Okay. (01:04:31): I take my iPhone and I balance it on the metal piece with the camera pointed at me, and I ask an AI to build me a training routine and watch me and tell me if I'm doing it right. Why do I need a personal trainer? Now, that might be complete nonsense, but that's how these things work. The stuff that you don't think is, you can't predict which things are going to be exposed necessarily. Or a lot of the big companies are things that didn't look like that would work and didn't look like I was exposed. The other side of this, of course, is this is one of the charts at the end of my presentation is comparing Uber and Airbnb, because this is like the cliche from Mark Andreessen that Uber doesn't sell software to taxi companies, Airbnb doesn't sell software to hotels. Okay, now let's go and look at the market impact. (01:05:16): Well, a whole bunch of cities were Uber demolished taxi business, and made it much bigger as well. The TAM became much bigger and everyone switched. Airbnb's impact hotels, if you actually go and look at the numbers, it's pretty marginal. They carved out this whole other business, and maybe they slowed down the growth of hotels a bit, but my wife flies to Milwaukee next week. She's going to land at eight o'clock at night. She wants to go to a hotel, she wants to have a room service, she needs a bath, she needs a gym at 6:00 in the morning, and then 7:00 in the morning, she's going to drive to the client's site. She's not going to stay in Airbnb. Absolutely zero chance she's going to stay in an Airbnb. And half of the hotel business is business travel. And as soon as you actually get into anything, then it gets complicated. (01:06:01): I remember somebody on social media said the problem with Benedict is his answer to everything is it depends. It's like, yeah, it does. It depends. So, it's back to my 1997 point. You can say some of this, but you have to have that humility.
turns.zh:
这简直就好像你没意识到那些无聊的体力劳动本可以实现自动化似的。你以为那是别的东西。说真的，我看过这类资料，美国政府有个叫ONET之类的数据集，试图分析每种职业，然后人们给它们打分，说“这个职业有X%暴露在AI技术下，而AI如今能完成Z%的相关工作”。我觉得这简直就是一堆稀释了的胡说八道。原因有两个。首先，这其实是逻辑系统的问题，也是专家系统的困境。专家系统的问题在于——对不了解的人来说——你试图识别一张猫的照片，于是开始搭建逻辑步骤。（01:03:14）比如做边缘检测器，然后第三层检测器，再做眼睛检测器和耳朵检测器，15年后你搞出700个步骤却还是不行。（01:03:25）当你试图拆解一个职业，分解哪些部分能自动化，哪些不能时，这种做法同样荒谬。你没法这样描述一个职业。但无论如何我们做不到。你不能对律所的资深合伙人说“嗯，他们17%的工作可以自动化”。这就是胡说八道。你做不到的。（01:03:43）不过谬论的另一面是谈论出租车司机。比如1997年我们讨论这个问题时，人们拿Uber来举例。想象一下1997年的我们会怎么预判哪些行业会被互联网淘汰？报纸会没事，因为能省下印刷费。这听起来像个笑话，但真有人这么说。报纸，互联网会让报纸受益。他们的印刷成本会降低。是的，但不行。另一方面，很明显出租车司机没法用互联网自动化。这和互联网毫无关系。或许你能有网络预约功能，但那样根本改变不了现状。当然，这完全扭转了局面。我前几天看到的例子是不会被AI影响的职业——私人教练。好吧，我拿起iPhone，把它放在有摄像头的金属支架上，让AI给我制定训练计划，看着我并告诉我是否做对了。我为什么需要私人教练？现在这可能完全是胡说八道，但这就是这些技术的运作方式。那些你觉得不会被AI影响的领域，你根本无法预测哪些会被暴露。很多大公司也是看起来行不通、看起来没暴露的。当然，另一个方面是我的演讲结尾的图表比较了Uber和Airbnb，因为这就是马克·安德森的经典观点——Uber不卖软件给出租车公司，Airbnb不卖软件给酒店。好吧，现在让我们看看市场影响。（01:05:16）很多城市的出租车业务被Uber摧毁，同时又变得更大。目标市场规模变得更大，大家都换了平台。Airbnb对酒店的影响，如果你实际去看数据，是相当有限的。他们开辟了整个新业务，或许让酒店增长放缓，但我妻子下周要飞去密尔沃基。她晚上8点落地，想住酒店，要客房服务，要洗澡，要健身房
早上6点，然后早上7点，她要开车去客户那里。她不会住在爱彼迎民宿里。绝对没有可能住在爱彼迎民宿里。酒店业务中有一半是商务旅行需求。而一旦涉及到具体细节，事情就会变得复杂起来。（01:06:01）：我记得社交媒体上有人说本尼迪克特的问题在于他对所有事情的回答都是“这得看情况”。是啊，就是得看情况。所以，这又回到了我1997年的观点。你可以说些相关的话，但你必须保持谦逊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to this phrase you use, presume radical uncertainty is a nice core thesis here. So knowing all this, just it's hard to tell. We don't know exactly where it's going. Things are going to change a lot, but it'll probably be okay broadly. Just a lot of people listening are pretty worried about their jobs and their careers, and how much the world changes. What would be a couple things you recommend people do knowing what you know to be more successful in this future?
turns.zh: 回到你提到的这句话，假设存在根本的不确定性，这确实是核心论点之一。综合这些情况来看，这确实很难预测。未来会发生巨大变化，但总体而言应该不会太糟糕。不过很多听众确实对自己的工作和职业前景感到担忧，也对世界变化的幅度心存疑虑。基于你的专业见解，你会给人们哪些建议，帮助他们在未来更成功？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Well, I should just wind back on what you just said. It's like, as Kim tells us, in the long run, we're all dead. So on average, nobody died in World War I. Great. But if you're a 19-year-old in 1914, you've got a one in three chances of not coming back. So yes, clearly there's a bunch of professions where this is a major question and particularly if you're an associate, or would've been thinking about being an associate, this is a major question. And it's very unclear how those professions are going to play out. It's very unclear what happens to the pyramid structure of professional services. The only answer I think one can have is, don't stick your head in the sand and say, "I hate all of this stuff," because that gives you a great feeling of moral superiority. And you can go on Bluesky and shout at everybody, chat at each other about how evil AI is like. Great, I'm happy for you, but that's not going to help. (01:07:48): What helps is you diving into this completely submerging yourself in it and coming at understanding what you can do with it, how this changes things, how you can be a great hire. And that may still not help. But if you're going to a law firm and they're like, well, we hired a hundred associates last year and this year we're only going to hire 50, go into the interview and say, "Well, I think AI is and I'm never going to use it," is probably not the right mood. So, that may not be particularly comforting, but I don't think there's an alternative, is you have to dive into this and absorb it, and internalize it and think about what it means, just as you and I did with mobile and with the internet.
turns.zh: 好的，我先回顾一下你刚才提到的观点。正如金所说，从长远看，我们都会死去。所以平均而言，第一次世界大战中没有人丧生。这很棒。但如果你是一名1914年的19岁新兵，回不来的概率高达三分之一。所以显然，许多职业领域都面临着重大挑战，特别是对于律师助理或有志于成为律师助理的人来说，这更是至关重要的问题。目前这些职业的未来走向尚不明朗，专业服务行业的金字塔结构将如何演变也存在诸多不确定。唯一的解决之道就是不要逃避现实，说：“我讨厌这一切。”这种道德优越感固然令人愉悦，但对现实毫无帮助。（01:07:48）真正有效的做法是深入研究，彻底理解人工智能将如何改变现状，如何提升自身竞争力。即便如此，可能依然难以改变现状。但如果你去律所面试时，说"我讨厌人工智能，从来不使用它"，这显然不是明智之举。所以，这或许不算安慰，但别无选择——你必须深入研究，理解其本质，思考其意义，正如我们当年研究移动互联网和互联网一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that is actually very actionable and very consistent advice on the podcast, is just, do stuff, build it, don't just sit around and pontificate and be pissed at what's happening. To close this out, I'm going to take us to AI Corner, a recurring corner of the podcast. And the question to you is just, what's one way you've used AI and use AI in your work or life that is really interesting, something that other people might be inspired by?
turns.zh: 我认为播客中最具可操作性的建议就是行动起来：动手实践，而不是空谈抱怨。要以此结束本期节目，让我们来聊聊AI Corner，这个播客的固定环节。我的问题是：你在工作或生活中应用过AI的哪些方式最有趣、最能启发他人？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I don't know. I struggle with this question, because I'm thought of the lawyer looking at ChatGPT. So, the stuff that I would do that I would automate are sort of precise information retrieval task, which is precisely the thing that this is kind of worse at. And that's not a criticism, it's just an observation. The kind of stuff that I would want a machine to do for me is the stuff that AI I can't do for me very, very, very well at the moment. I use it for proofreading, I use it for images, I used it redecorating my apartment, that worked fantastic, you're aware at that. Here's a picture of this room, repaint it at this light and this table and this rug. No change color of the rug. There's a kind of class of stuff where it works. But I mean, a couple of years ago, somebody said AI is good at stuff that computers are bad at and bad at stuff that computers are good at. (01:09:49): And I struggle to find many examples of those where I need it. But then I'm kind of a unique, weird job. I sit at my desk all day trying to synthesize a whole bunch of other stuff into a whole bunch of new ideas. That's not particularly common way for people to spend their time. I struggle to find AI use cases. I am the accountant looking at the spreadsheet and thinking, "Well, that's very clever, and this is clearly going to completely transform everything, but I actually don't make spreadsheets every day."
turns.zh: 我不知道。我在回答这个问题时很纠结，因为我一想到律师使用ChatGPT的情景，就会联想到这类技术在精准信息检索方面存在的局限性，而这恰恰是AI最不擅长的地方。这并非批评，只是客观观察。我希望AI能为我自动完成的任务，恰恰是目前AI还做不到的——比如校对文本、处理图像、重新布置家居（我用它重新布置房间的效果很棒，你可能见过那张照片：重新粉刷房间、调整灯光、摆放桌子和地毯，但地毯颜色不变）。这类应用场景确实有效。但几年前有人说过，AI擅长做计算机不擅长的事，却不擅长做计算机擅长的事。（01:09:49）我很难找到这类实际应用案例。不过我从事的工作比较独特、有点怪异——整天坐在办公桌前，试图将各种信息整合成新的创意。这类工作方式并不常见。我很难找到AI的实用场景。就像会计师看着电子表格，心想：“这技术真厉害，肯定能彻底改变一切，但我又不是每天都在做表格。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I went to a standup comedy show of Pete Holmes, I don't know if you know him. And he made this joke that we want AI to clean the poop off the street and do all these hard things that nobody wants to do, but instead it's like, "Oh, let me help you write. Let me help you create imagery." It's like this bohemian. It's like, "No, I don't want to do all these ugly things. I want to be creative, make art."
turns.zh: 我去看过皮特·霍尔姆斯的单口喜剧表演，不知道你是否了解他。他开玩笑说，我们希望AI能清理街道上的粪便，处理那些没人愿意做但又必须做的脏活累活，结果AI却偏偏要帮你写作、制作图像。这太不务实了。就像文艺青年，总想说：“不，我不想做那些丑陋的活儿，我要创造艺术。”

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I mean, there's variations of all of this. It's like I don't want the AI to do the stuff I do for fun. I want it to do the boring stuff that I don't do for fun. And finding that mesh. I mean, joking apart, this is going to come back to my chatbot point, that the chatbot is a blank screen in a jagged edge. And what am I supposed to do and what will work? And that's a big problem. And the solution to that problem is to wrap it in use cases. Part of it is also like AI just disappears. So most of what I write now I dictate. I dictate as a voicemail, and that's automatically transcribed. Is that still AI or is that just voice recognition? There's probably an LLM in there. Okay. So maybe that's AI. Well, okay. So what? At a certain point, it's just automation.
turns.zh: 是啊。这类问题有各种变体。我不想让AI做我用来娱乐的事，而是处理那些无聊又不怎么有趣的任务。关键在于找到平衡点。说实话，这又回到了我之前提到的聊天机器人问题——它就像一块空白的屏幕，边缘参差不齐。我该怎么做才能成功？这确实是个大问题。解决办法就是用具体的应用场景来框定它。还有个问题是，AI往往神秘消失。比如我现在写的大部分内容都是口述录音，直接转换成文字。这还是AI吗？还是语音识别？里面可能有大语言模型。好吧，也许这就是AI。管他呢，自动化就是自动化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you use for that, for voice transcription?
turns.zh: 你用什么工具进行语音转录？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: So, I actually find that Apple Notes, the app or the one built into the iPhone works fine. I mean, I'm conscious of the people want others, but I mean, I dictate it. There it is. It worked. So, I'm happy with that.
turns.zh: 其实我发现苹果备忘录这个应用，或者iPhone自带的备忘录功能就很不错。我会口述录音，直接转换成文字。效果不错。所以我挺满意的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. Is there anything else that you wanted to share? Anything else you want to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 好的。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后一个问题：你还有什么想分享的吗？有什么想留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: No, I think I've monologued plenty, and I've gone through a bunch of stuff in the deck. Go read the deck, and sign up to my newsletter, and then you will get in many more mags of brilliant Benedict Evans' wisdom, some of which may even be useful. Someone unsubscribed for my newsletter and they said, "You didn't give me any actionable stock ideas." And I'm like, "Well, on one level, that's completely true. On the other level, maybe not."
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得我已经说得够多了，而且我已经在演示文稿中讲了很多内容。去看看演示文稿，然后订阅我的新闻通讯，这样你就能收到更多本尼迪克特·埃文斯（Benedict Evans）精彩观点的杂志，其中有些甚至可能对你有用。有个人取消了我的新闻通讯订阅，还说：“你没有给我任何可行的股票投资建议。”我回应道：“嗯，从某种程度上说，这完全正确。但从另一个角度看，也许并非如此。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, Benedict, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，本尼迪克特，我们现在要进行激动人心的闪电问答环节了。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，哪两三本书是你最常向别人推荐的？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: It's a tough one for me, because I just read an enormous amount of books and then I can't remember which ones I've read. I sometimes often joke that there's a classic British comedy from the late 19th century called Three Men in a Boat, which is like my I Ching. We're having trouble hanging a picture. Well, there's a section about that. We're having trouble doing this. Oh, well, there's a story about that, all of which are hilarious. So Three Men in a Boat is my I Ching. (01:12:53): There's a book by, I think William Cronon, about the Economic History of Chicago, which is fascinating and actually very relevant to technology, because it's talking basically about standardization and packetization, and logistics, and channel conflict, and network dynamics, and network neutrality. So, when the meat packers of Chicago reach the point that it's cheaper to ship a cow from New York to Chicago, kill it, pack it, and then ship it back to New York than to kill it in New York, and the pricing of refrigerator cars, and it's exactly like reading about broadband. It's all the same kind of... So those kinds of business issues, which is fascinating. (01:13:27): What else have I read? I don't know. Read books, read different books, generally read books for grownups. Please read something other than Lord of the Rings, if you're going to name another company. I saw this one and what was the latest Peter Thiel company. I was like, "Read another book." Everything is named after a character from this one book. There's more than one book in the world. There is more than one book than all about science fiction. Read about different things, read about things you don't know about.
turns.zh: 这对我来说挺难的，因为我读了太多书，根本记不清读过哪些书了。我有时会开玩笑说，19世纪末有一部经典英国喜剧叫《三人同舟》，这就像我的《易经》。我们挂画遇到困难。嗯，书里有相关段落。我们做这件事遇到困难。哦，书里也有相关故事，全都超级搞笑。所以《三人同舟》就是我的《易经》。（01:12:53）：还有一本威廉·克罗农（William Cronon）写的关于芝加哥经济史的书，非常精彩，而且与科技相关性极强，因为它主要讲标准化和打包、物流、渠道冲突和网络中立性。比如芝加哥的肉类加工商发现从纽约运牛到芝加哥宰杀后再运回纽约，比在纽约宰杀更便宜时，还有冷藏车定价的问题，这简直就像在读宽带相关内容。都是同一类型的……所以这些商业问题非常有趣。（01:13:27）：我还读了什么？我不知道。多读点书，读不同的书，总之读些适合成年人读的书。如果你要提另一个公司，那我建议别提《指环王》了。我看到皮特·泰尔（Peter Thiel）最新创办的公司，我当时就说：「再读本书吧。」结果所有公司都以那本书里的角色命名。世界上不止一本书。也不止一本科幻小说。多读些不同领域的书，了解你不了解的领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of along those lines, you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I don't know. I've dropped so badly off the current media treadmill, and I just spend most of my time watching classics, which are always the ones that you're supposed to have seen and that all seem intimidating. And then you watch them and you're like, "Oh, that was actually really good." I watched The Seventh Seal recently, which is one of those Woody Allen, terrifying boring movies, and it was brilliant. It was really interesting, and it's like it's only like an hour. So, go watch one of those movies that you are supposed to have seen, or hadn't seen.
turns.zh: 不知道。我已经严重脱离了当前的媒体潮流，大部分时间都在看经典影片，而这些经典影片往往是被视为必看之作，但看起来又让人望而生畏。结果你看了之后会发现：“哦，这部电影其实挺不错的。” 我最近看了《第七封印》，这部伍迪·艾伦（Woody Allen）的电影，超级无聊又恐怖，但确实很棒。它只有一个小时左右，所以去看看这些被视为必看的电影，或者那些你没看过的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite recent product that you recently discovered that I really love. Could be a gadget, could be an app.
turns.zh: 最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？可以是一款小玩意儿，或者一款应用。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I was speaking at a partner meeting for a company earlier this week. Monday, no, last week, and met the founder of the company who has a very famous... The CEO of the company has a famous name and admired his shoes, and didn't say anything, but then went in Google half an hour later. "Yeah, okay, I'll buy a pair of this."
turns.zh: 本周早些时候，我在一家公司的合作伙伴会议上发言。周一，不，是上周，我见到了公司创始人，他非常有名……公司的首席执行官名声在外，我很欣赏他的鞋子，但当时没说什么，不过半小时后就去谷歌上搜了一下。“嗯，好的，我要买一双。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you want to share the brand or you want to keep it secret? Okay, we'll keep it secret.
turns.zh: 你想分享这个品牌还是保密？好的，我们保密吧。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I don't know. I think one comes in waves of new products, and you get into waves of new things. And when's the last time there was a cool app, iPhone apps, all that white space went. I mean, it's partly a function of product ships, a platform chips. All the white space went for cool new apps, and now we haven't quite got... Actually, this is to the earlier point, we don't have breakout a consumer AI apps yet, but I think because of marginal cost more than anything else, you can't make it free and get 50 million users and then have a revenue bottle. But we don't have those breakout things yet.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我觉得新产品会一波接一波地涌现，你也会跟上新事物的潮流。上次有酷炫的应用程序，比如iPhone应用，所有那些空白区域都被填满了。我的意思是，这在一定程度上取决于产品设计和平台开发。所有空白区域都被酷炫的新应用占据了，而现在我们还没有……实际上，这回到了前面提到的问题，我们还没有突破性的消费者人工智能应用，但我认为主要是因为边际成本的原因，你不能免费提供服务然后获得5000万用户，再面临收入瓶颈。但我们目前还没有这样的突破性产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For consumer.
turns.zh: 针对消费者的。

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: For consumer, no. I keep getting these ads for voice recorders. Somebody's selling a business card size hardware voice recorder. But I didn't get it. I've got the voice recorder on my phone.
turns.zh: 针对消费者的，不行。我老是收到录音笔的广告。有人在卖名片大小的硬件录音笔。但我没买。我手机上就有录音功能了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. All kinds of cool stuff coming. Okay. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to often in work or in life?
turns.zh: 是的。各种酷炫的东西即将到来。好的。再问两个问题。你有没有最喜欢的的人生格言，在工作或生活中经常回味的？

turns.en: I suppose both mentioned earlier, apparently, I mostly say it depends.
turns.zh: 我想前面提到过的，显然，我大多会说这取决于情况。

turns.en: That's going to be the title.
turns.zh: 这将是标题。

turns.en: It'll probably be okay.
turns.zh: 应该没问题。

turns.en: Yeah. Okay. That's the vibe I get. I like that. I like that. It's probably going to be okay. Not for sure. Okay. Final question. I saw someone that you'll own a lot of old phones. Is that true?
turns.zh: 是的。好的。这就是我的感觉。我喜欢这样。我喜欢这样。应该没问题。不确定。好的。最后一个问题。我听说你有很多旧手机。这是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: It is, yes. I mean, I was a telecoms analyst and mobile analyst and I kept all my phones up to a point. Now they're kind of uninteresting. But as you may remember, before the iPhone, particularly outside the USA, there was this huge creativity and expansion in what phones looked like, because everyone was basically innovating around a little teeny, tiny gray square. So everyone was trying to differentiate from everything else, before it kind of resulted. It's kind of like cars, actually. It's like cars before street, before wind tunnels, cars all look different. And everyone's trying to innovate around, because you've got the same four wheels, and the same engine, and everyone's trying to differentiate based on the shape. And then everything converges on one shape, and it's kind of the same with phones. Everything converged on one shape. Before that, there was all this innovation. So yeah, I have a whole bunch of PDAs, and smartphones, and things like that.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我是说，我曾是电信分析师和移动设备分析师，之前一直保留着我的手机。现在它们变得没什么意思了。但你可能还记得，在iPhone问世之前，尤其是在美国以外，手机外观设计和功能扩展方面曾有过巨大的创造力和创新，因为当时每个人都在围绕一个小小的灰色方块进行创新。于是每个人都在努力使自己的产品与众不同，直到最终形成了一种标准。这就像汽车行业一样。汽车在没有街道赛车、风洞测试之前，样子各不相同。每个人都在围绕四个轮子和一个引擎进行创新，努力通过外形来区分产品。然后最终都趋于一致。手机行业也是如此。在那之前，创新层出不穷。所以是的，我有各种PDA、智能手机之类的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many phones are we talking about?
turns.zh: 我们说的是多少部手机？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: I don't know, like 20 or 30.
turns.zh: 我不知道，大概20到30部吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay. It's not so crazy. What's the oldest one? What's the oldest one you got?
turns.zh: 好的。好的。这倒不算太夸张。最旧的手机是哪部？你拥有的最旧的手机是哪部？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: So I have one of those, I should have usually told me I'd have got the box down, I have one of those Ericsson shark fin flip phones from '98 or something, which is very vogue. Again, hardware design, visual design, trying to differentiate. I've got an iMade phone from 2001, and a JPhone phone from 2001 that has a camera. So I came back from Japan in 2001 and my phone had a color screen and a camera. And I just had endless client meetings and people just wanted to see the phone with a color screen. It's mind-blowing. Didn't work outside Japan. So, I plugged it in the other day. It still charges up. I mean, clearly I can't do anything with it. I mean, there's a little bit of an analogy in there as well in that we thought there'd be all these different shapes and sizes. (01:17:52): And before the iPhone, people kind of imagined, "Well, some people will have a little pocket PC, and some people have a keyboard, and you have folding..." There were all these different ideas for what it would look like. And we didn't realize it was all going to converge on one device.
turns.zh: 嗯，我也有过类似的经历。我本该早点告诉自己要把手机放下的，那部98年左右的爱立信鲨鱼鳍翻盖手机实在太时髦了。再说回硬件设计和视觉设计，人们总想在这些方面脱颖而出。我还有2001年的iMade手机和2001年的JPhone手机，后者带有摄像头。我2001年从日本回来时，手机就有了彩色屏幕和摄像头。但当时参加客户会议时，大家只想看看带彩色屏幕的手机。真是令人惊叹。不过这手机在日本以外用不了。前几天我试着充电，发现还能充进电。显然我现在用不了它了。这里有个小比喻——当时我们以为手机会有各种各样的形状和尺寸。（01:17:52）在iPhone问世之前，人们想象着“有些人会用小型掌上电脑，有些人用键盘，还有折叠屏手机……”各种设计想法层出不穷。但我们没意识到最终会统一成一种设备。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Benedict, this was amazing. I learned a ton. I feel better after this conversation. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online? Where do they find this presentation? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 本尼迪克特，这次交流太棒了。我收获满满。听完感觉好多了。最后两个问题：大家在哪里能找到你的在线资料？哪里能看到这场演讲？听众如何能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Benedict Evans
turns.en: If you can Google me, as I always say, my parents had good SEO. So, Google Benedict Evans. And so there's a website where I publish all the presentations that I've done. And sign up for my newsletter, which comes out every week. Otherwise, how can they be useful to me? I'm always trying to understand stuff and I'm always trying to ask different questions. The worst thing in tech is to carry on talking about the same stuff. It's like the moment you really understand something, it's the moment you have to push onto something else. And so I'm always trying to think like, "No, am I just talking about the same thing over and over again?" Last year I just spent probably too much time saying, "But these models still hallucinate. Stop telling me they don't hallucinate." And they do. They still hallucinate. You push them, push them a little bit further, any question and you'll still get like, "No, that's not true," but that doesn't mean they're not useful. So you have to keep pushing myself. (01:19:06): So that's always that the challenge for me, is how do I push? And then yes, if you want me to come and present to your board in the Caribbean, then let me know.
turns.zh: 如果你能在谷歌上搜到我（就像我常说的，我父母的SEO做得很棒），直接搜索“本尼迪克特·埃文斯”。我有一个网站，里面发布了所有我做过的演讲。也可以订阅我的每周通讯。至于怎么帮到我？我总在努力理解新事物，提出不同的问题。科技领域最忌讳的就是老是重复谈论同样的东西。当你真正理解某件事时，就是该转向新领域的时候了。所以我总在自问：“我是不是一直在重复讲同样的内容？”去年我花了太多时间说：“但这些模型还是会出错。别再跟我说它们不会出错了。” 但它们确实会出错。再深挖一点任何问题，得到的回答都是“不，不对”，但这并不意味着它们没用。你得不断鞭策自己。
